cor-best-fitting-subspace.title: The best-fitting subspace
cor-best-fitting-subspace.html: Let a1,…,an∈Fm be the columns of A, and let 1≤k≤p. Among all subspaces S⊆Fm with dim⁡S≤k, the total squared distance D(S):=∑j=1nd(aj,S)2 is smallest for S=span(u1,…,uk), and its smallest value is ∑i>kσi2.

cor-fischer-inequality.title: Fischer’s Inequality
cor-fischer-inequality.html:
Let M=(ABB∗C)∈Mk+l(F) with M⪰0, where A∈Mk(F) and C∈Ml(F). Then

detM≤detA⋅detC.

If M≻0, equality holds if and only if B=0.

cor-orthogonal-idempotent-unique.title: One Orthogonal Projection per Subspace
cor-orthogonal-idempotent-unique.html: Let U be a subspace of a finite-dimensional inner product space V. Among the projections of V with image U — one for each complement of U, by @thm-projection-direct-sum — exactly one is self-adjoint, namely PU.

cor-svd-four-subspaces.title: The Four Fundamental Subspaces from the Compact Form
cor-svd-four-subspaces.title_html: The Four Fundamental Subspaces from the Compact Form
cor-svd-four-subspaces.html:

  2. (ur+1,…,um) is an orthonormal basis of kerA∗;
  3. (v1,…,vr) is an orthonormal basis of imA∗;
  4. (vr+1,…,vn) is an orthonormal basis of kerA.

cor-unitary-nearest.title_html: The Polar Factor Is the Nearest Unitary Matrix
cor-unitary-nearest.html: Let A∈Mn(C) with polar decomposition A=W|A|. Then ‖A−W‖F≤‖A−Q‖Ffor every unitary Q∈Mn(C), and the minimum value is (‖A‖F2+n−2∑iσi)1/2. If A is invertible, W is the only unitary matrix attaining the minimum.

def-generalized-eigenvalue.title: Generalized eigenvalue
def-generalized-eigenvalue.html: Let A,B∈Mn(F). A scalar λ∈F is a generalized eigenvalue of the pair (A,B) if Bx=λAxfor some x≠0, and such an x is a generalized eigenvector for λ. The family of matrices B−λA is called the pencil of the pair.

def-hadamard-product.title: Hadamard Product
def-hadamard-product.html:
Let A,B∈Mm×n(F). Their Hadamard product, or entrywise product, is the matrix A∘B∈Mm×n(F) with

(A∘B)ij=aijbijfor all i,j.

def-k-volume.title: Volume of a list
def-k-volume.html: Let (v1,…,vk) be a list in an inner product space V over F. Its k-dimensional volume vol(v1,…,vk)≥0 is defined recursively by vol(v1)=‖v1‖,vol(v1,…,vk)=vol(v1,…,vk−1)⋅d(vk,Uk−1), where Uk−1=span(v1,…,vk−1) and d(⋅,⋅) is the distance of @def-distance-to-subspace.

def-loewner-order.title: The Loewner order
def-loewner-order.html: Let A,B∈Mn(F) be Hermitian. Write A⪰Bto meanA−B⪰0, and A≻B to mean A−B≻0. This relation on the set of Hermitian matrices is the Loewner order.

def-matrix-absolute-value.title: Absolute Value of a Matrix
def-matrix-absolute-value.html: Let A∈Mm×n(F). The absolute value of A is |A|:=(A∗A)1/2∈Mn(F), the unique positive semidefinite square root of A∗A.

def-positive-semidefinite.title: Positive Semidefinite and Positive Definite
def-positive-semidefinite.html:
Let A∈Mn(F). Then A is positive semidefinite, written A⪰0, if

  1. A is Hermitian, that is A∗=A (over R: symmetric, A⊤=A); and
  2. ⟨Ax,x⟩≥0 for every x∈Fn.

It is positive definite, written A≻0, if (P1) holds and ⟨Ax,x⟩>0 for every non-zero x∈Fn.

The same words apply to an operator T∈L(V) on a finite-dimensional inner product space: T is positive semidefinite if T∗=T and ⟨Tv,v⟩≥0 for every v∈V, and positive definite if the inequality is strict for v≠0.

def-pseudoinverse.title: Moore–Penrose pseudoinverse
def-pseudoinverse.html: Let A∈Mm×n(F) and let A=UΣV∗ be a singular value decomposition (@thm-svd), so that U∈Mm(F) and V∈Mn(F) are unitary and Σ∈Mm×n(F) has the singular values σ1,…,σp on its diagonal and zeros elsewhere. Let Σ+∈Mn×m(F) be the matrix with (Σ+)ii={σi−1,σi>0,0,σi=0, for 1≤i≤p, and all other entries 0. The Moore–Penrose pseudoinverse of A is A+:=VΣ+U∗∈Mn×m(F).

def-singular-values.title: Singular Values
def-singular-values.html: Let A∈Mm×n(F) and put p=min(m,n). Let λ1≥λ2≥⋯≥λn≥0 be the eigenvalues of A∗A∈Mn(F), listed with multiplicity in decreasing order. The singular values of A are σi(A):=λi(i=1,…,p), so that σ1(A)≥σ2(A)≥⋯≥σp(A)≥0. We write σi when A is clear.

def-truncated-svd.title: Truncated singular value decomposition
def-truncated-svd.html: For 0≤k≤p, the rank-k truncation of A relative to the chosen singular value decomposition A=UΣV∗ (@thm-svd) is Ak:=∑i=1kσiuivi∗, with A0=0; for k≥p we set Ak=A.

exm-pseudoinverse-first-examples.title: Five pseudoinverses
exm-pseudoinverse-first-examples.html:
1. A invertible. Then m=n=r, Σ is invertible and Σ+=Σ−1, so A+=VΣ−1U∗=(UΣV∗)−1=A−1. The pseudoinverse extends the inverse, which is the first thing it had to do.
  2. A=0∈Mm×n(F). Every singular value is 0, so Σ+=0 and A+=0∈Mn×m(F). The degenerate case is worth keeping in mind: the pseudoinverse of the worst possible matrix is not undefined, it is zero, which is what “invert nothing, kill everything” means.
  3. Diagonal. diag(2,0,5)+=diag(12,0,15). The zero is left where it is.
  4. A single non-zero column a∈Mn×1(F). Here σ1=‖a‖, u1=a/‖a‖ and v1=1, so a+=a∗/‖a‖2, a row vector. Then a+a=1 but aa+=aa∗/‖a‖2 is the orthogonal projection onto span(a).
  5. A=(1111). This is σ1u1v1∗ with σ1=2 and u1=v1=12(1,1), since 2u1v1∗=2⋅12(1111)=A. Hence A+=12v1u1∗=14(1111).

exr-polar-decomposition-c1.html:
Let A∈Mn(C).

  1. Suppose A=QP with Q unitary and P⪰0. Prove that P=|A|. (Invertibility is not assumed.)
  2. Deduce that A is unitary if and only if |A|=I.

exr-polar-decomposition-c2.title: C2: Normality through the polar factors
exr-polar-decomposition-c2.title_html: C2: Normality through the polar factors
exr-polar-decomposition-c2.html:
Let A∈Mn(C) be invertible with polar decomposition A=W|A|. Prove that the following are equivalent.

  1. A is normal.
  2. |A|=|A∗|.
  3. W|A|=|A|W.

exr-polar-decomposition-c3.title: C3: Complex symmetric matrices are transposed squares
exr-polar-decomposition-c3.title_html: C3: Complex symmetric matrices are transposed squares
exr-polar-decomposition-c3.html:
Let A∈Mn(C) be symmetric and invertible.

  1. Using @thm-takagi, prove that A=B⊤B for some invertible B∈Mn(C).
  2. Show that over R the analogous statement is false unless A is positive definite, and give a 1×1 witness.
  3. Explain in one sentence why (a) and (b) do not contradict each other.

exr-positive-definite-matrices-a1.title: A1
exr-positive-definite-matrices-a1.html:
1. State the definition of A⪰0 and of A≻0, including every quantifier and the field.
  2. Explain why clause (P1) cannot be dropped from the real definition, with a concrete matrix.
  3. True or false: if A is Hermitian and every leading principal minor of A is ≥0, then A⪰0. Justify your answer.
  4. Write down the three conditions of the 2×2 test for A⪰0.
  5. Name the item of @thm-psd-characterizations that says every positive semidefinite matrix is a Gram matrix.

exr-positive-definite-matrices-b1.title: B1: Determine the definiteness
exr-positive-definite-matrices-b1.html:
For each matrix below, determine whether it is positive definite, positive semidefinite but not positive definite, or neither. Justify your answer.

  1. (2112) over R.
  2. (000−1) over R.
  3. (2−10−12−10−12) over R.
  4. The all-ones matrix J∈M3(R).
  5. (01−10) over R.
  6. (21+i1−i1) over C.

exr-positive-definite-matrices-b2.title: B2: A parameter
exr-positive-definite-matrices-b2.html: For which t∈R is A(t)=(1t0t2t0t3) positive definite? Justify your answer.

exr-positive-definite-matrices-b3.title: B3: The inverse of a positive definite matrix
exr-positive-definite-matrices-b3.title_html: B3: The inverse of a positive definite matrix
exr-positive-definite-matrices-b3.html: Let A∈Mn(F) with A≻0. Prove that A is invertible and that A−1≻0.

exr-positive-definite-matrices-c1.title: C1: Zero trace forces zero
exr-positive-definite-matrices-c1.html:
Let A∈Mn(F) with A⪰0.

  1. Prove that aii≥0 for every i, and that trA≥0.
  2. Prove that if trA=0 then A=0.
  3. Deduce that if A⪰0 and −A⪰0, then A=0.

exr-positive-definite-matrices-c2.title: C2: The cone of positive matrices
exr-positive-definite-matrices-c2.title_html: C2: The cone of positive matrices
exr-positive-definite-matrices-c2.html:
Let Pn⊆Mn(F) be the set of positive semidefinite matrices.

  1. Prove that if A,B∈Pn and c≥0 is real, then A+B∈Pn and cA∈Pn. (A set with these two properties is a convex cone: it contains (1−t)A+tB for 0≤t≤1 as well.)
  2. Prove that Pn contains no line through 0: if A∈Pn and −A∈Pn then A=0.
  3. Prove that Pn is closed under congruence: if A∈Pn and S∈Mn(F), then S∗AS∈Pn. Give an example showing that Pn is not closed under multiplication.

Hint for (c): for the example, two positive semidefinite matrices whose product is not even Hermitian will do.

exr-positive-definite-matrices-c3.title: C3: The largest entry sits on the diagonal
exr-positive-definite-matrices-c3.title_html: C3: The largest entry sits on the diagonal
exr-positive-definite-matrices-c3.html:
Let A∈Mn(F) with A⪰0.

  1. Prove that |aij|2≤aiiajj for all i,j.
  2. Deduce that if aii=0 for some i, then the whole i-th row and i-th column of A are zero.
  3. Deduce that maxi,j|aij|=maxiaii.

Hint for (a): look at a 2×2 principal submatrix.

exr-projections-revisited-a1.title: A1
exr-projections-revisited-a1.html:
1. Define what it means for P∈L(V) to be a projection, and what it means for it to be the orthogonal projection onto a subspace U. Which of the two definitions needs an inner product?
  2. State three conditions on a projection P, each equivalent to “P is an orthogonal projection”.
  3. Determine whether the following is correct, and justify your answer: if ‖Pv‖≤‖v‖ for some non-zero v, then the projection P is orthogonal.
  4. Determine whether the following is correct, and justify your answer: every projection of rank r on an n-dimensional inner product space has matrix Ir⊕0 in some orthonormal basis.

exr-projections-revisited-b1.title: B1: Which are orthogonal projections?
exr-projections-revisited-b1.html:
Determine which of the following matrices are projections, and among those, which are orthogonal projections. Justify your answer. For the oblique ones over R, find the angle between image and kernel.

  1. A=15(1224) on R2.
  2. B=(10−20) on R2.
  3. C=(1111) on R2.
  4. D=(1i00) on C2.

exr-projections-revisited-b2.title: B2: Putting a projection in canonical form
exr-projections-revisited-b2.title_html: B2: Putting a projection in canonical form
exr-projections-revisited-b2.html:
Let A=(010010001) act on R3 with the dot product.

  1. Verify that A is a projection and find imA and kerA.
  2. Find an orthonormal basis B of R3 as in @thm-idempotent-canonical-form and write down [A]B.
  3. Hence determine whether A is an orthogonal projection, and find rankA without row reducing.

exr-projections-revisited-b3.title: B3: The complementary projection
exr-projections-revisited-b3.html:
Let P∈L(V) be a projection on a finite-dimensional inner product space, with U=imP.

  1. Prove that P is an orthogonal projection if and only if idV−P is.
  2. Prove that in that case idV−P=PU⊥.

Hint: @exr-projections-and-trace-b2 identifies the image and the kernel of idV−P.

exr-projections-revisited-c1.title: C1: Products of orthogonal projections
exr-projections-revisited-c1.html:
Let P and Q be orthogonal projections on a finite-dimensional inner product space V, with images U and W.

  1. Prove that PQ is an orthogonal projection if and only if PQ=QP.
  2. Suppose PQ=QP. Prove that PQ=PU∩W.
  3. Give an explicit example of two orthogonal projections on R2 whose product is not a projection.

exr-projections-revisited-c2.title: C2: The Frobenius norm detects obliqueness
exr-projections-revisited-c2.title_html: C2: The Frobenius norm detects obliqueness
exr-projections-revisited-c2.html:
Let P∈Mn(F) be idempotent, of rank r.

  1. Prove that ‖P‖F2≥r.
  2. Prove that equality holds if and only if P is an orthogonal projection.

Hint: the canonical form of @thm-idempotent-canonical-form, together with the invariance of the Frobenius norm under a unitary change of orthonormal basis.

exr-projections-revisited-c3.title: C3: How far an oblique projection can stretch
exr-projections-revisited-c3.title_html: C3: How far an oblique projection can stretch
exr-projections-revisited-c3.html:
Let P be a projection of rank r on an n-dimensional inner product space V over F, with 0<r<n, and let X be the block of @thm-idempotent-canonical-form, with largest singular value σ1=σ1(X).

  1. Prove that ‖Xz‖≤σ1‖z‖ for every z∈Fn−r, with equality for some z≠0.
  2. Prove that the largest value of ‖Pv‖ over unit vectors v∈V is 1+σ12.
  3. Deduce the two-dimensional formula 1+|x|2 of the text, and state what the answer becomes when P is an orthogonal projection.

exr-pseudoinverse-a1.title: A1
exr-pseudoinverse-a1.html:
1. Define A+ in terms of a singular value decomposition of A (@thm-svd), and say what size it is.
  2. State the four Penrose conditions, and say what @thm-penrose-conditions asserts about them.
  3. What are AA+ and A+A? Under what condition on A is the second of them In?
  4. Write down 0+ for the zero matrix 0∈Mm×n(F), and A+ for an invertible A.
  5. True or false: (AB)+=B+A+ whenever the product AB is defined. Justify your answer.

exr-pseudoinverse-b1.title: B1: Four pseudoinverses
exr-pseudoinverse-b1.html:
Compute A+ for each of the following, stating which method you used.

  1. A=diag(3,0,0,4)∈M4(R);
  2. A=(1,2,2)⊤∈M3×1(R);
  3. A=(1224)∈M2(R);
  4. A=(101011)∈M2×3(R).

exr-pseudoinverse-b2.title: B2: A system that is both inconsistent and underdetermined
exr-pseudoinverse-b2.title_html: B2: A system that is both inconsistent and underdetermined
exr-pseudoinverse-b2.html: Let A=(122412),b=(1,4,1). Compute A+ and xmin=A+b. Verify that Axmin is the orthogonal projection of b onto col(A), and compare ‖xmin‖ with the norm of one other least-squares solution.

exr-pseudoinverse-b3.title: B3: Checking a candidate
exr-pseudoinverse-b3.html: Let A=(101101) and X=13(21−1−112). Verify the four Penrose conditions for X, and hence find the minimum-norm least-squares solution of Ax=(1,2,3).

exr-pseudoinverse-c1.title: C1: Pseudoinverses of \A^{*}\A
exr-pseudoinverse-c1.title_html: C1: Pseudoinverses of A∗A
exr-pseudoinverse-c1.html:
Let A∈Mm×n(F).

  1. Prove that (A∗A)+=A+(A+)∗.
  2. Deduce that A+=(A∗A)+A∗, the formula (A∗A)−1A∗ with the inverse replaced by the pseudoinverse.

Hint: use a singular value decomposition and reduce each identity to an identity between diagonal matrices.

exr-pseudoinverse-c2.title: C2: When the reversal rule does hold
exr-pseudoinverse-c2.title_html: C2: When the reversal rule does hold
exr-pseudoinverse-c2.html: Let A∈Mm×n(F) with rankA=n and B∈Mn×q(F) with rankB=n. Prove that (AB)+=B+A+. Hint: write both pseudoinverses with the formulas of @thm-pseudoinverse-properties (e) and verify the Penrose conditions for the product.

exr-pseudoinverse-c3.title: C3: When the pseudoinverse is the adjoint
exr-pseudoinverse-c3.title_html: C3: When the pseudoinverse is the adjoint
exr-pseudoinverse-c3.html:
Let A∈Mm×n(F).

  1. Prove that A+=A∗ if and only if AA∗A=A.
  2. Deduce that A+=A∗ if and only if every non-zero singular value of A equals 1.
  3. Give an example of such an A in M2(R) which is neither unitary nor an orthogonal projection.

exr-schur-product-theorem-a1.title: A1
exr-schur-product-theorem-a1.html:
1. Define A∘B, and say what shapes the two factors must have.
  2. What is A∘I? What is A∘J?
  3. State the Schur product theorem.
  4. True or false: if A≻0, then the matrix with entries 1/aij (assuming no entry is 0) is positive definite. Justify your answer.
  5. What does Oppenheim’s inequality say when B=I?

exr-schur-product-theorem-b1.title: B1: Compute and decide
exr-schur-product-theorem-b1.html:
For each pair below, compute A∘B and determine whether it is positive definite, positive semidefinite but not definite, or neither. Say in each case whether @thm-schur-product applies.

  1. A=(1111), B=(1111).
  2. A=(1111), B=(1221).
  3. A=(2112), B=(3−1−11).

exr-schur-product-theorem-b2.title: B2: Entrywise squares
exr-schur-product-theorem-b2.html:
Let A=(111122123).

  1. Show that A≻0.
  2. Compute A∘A, the matrix of squared entries, and verify that it is positive definite.
  3. Explain why (b) needed no computation.

exr-schur-product-theorem-c1.title: C1: Polynomials applied entrywise
exr-schur-product-theorem-c1.html:
Let A∈Mn(F) with A⪰0.

  1. Prove that the entrywise power A∘m, with (i,j) entry aijm, is positive semidefinite for every integer m≥1.
  2. Let p(x)=c0+c1x+⋯+cdxd have non-negative real coefficients. Prove that the matrix p∘(A) with (i,j) entry p(aij) is positive semidefinite.
  3. Give an example of A⪰0 and a polynomial p with a negative coefficient for which p∘(A) is not positive semidefinite.

exr-schur-product-theorem-c2.title: C2: The product of the determinants
exr-schur-product-theorem-c2.title_html: C2: The product of the determinants
exr-schur-product-theorem-c2.html:
Let A,B∈Mn(F) with A⪰0 and B⪰0. Prove that

det(A∘B) ≥ detA⋅detB.

Is the inequality ever an equality with both matrices positive definite?

exr-schur-product-theorem-c3.title: C3: The rank of an entrywise product
exr-schur-product-theorem-c3.title_html: C3: The rank of an entrywise product
exr-schur-product-theorem-c3.html:
Let A,B∈Mn(F) with A⪰0 and B⪰0, of ranks r and s. Prove that

rank(A∘B)≤rs.

Hint: how many terms in the proof of @thm-schur-product (a) are actually non-zero?

exr-simultaneous-diagonalization-a1.title: A1
exr-simultaneous-diagonalization-a1.html:
1. Define what it means for two matrices to be congruent, and say which of similarity and congruence is the natural relation for a form.
  2. State @thm-simultaneous-congruence, with all hypotheses.
  3. Name two differences between @thm-simultaneous-congruence and @thm-simultaneous-unitary-diagonalization.
  4. Determine whether the following statement is correct, and justify your answer: the generalized eigenvalues of (A,B) are eigenvalues of B.
  5. For A≻0 and B self-adjoint, what inner product makes A−1B self-adjoint?

exr-simultaneous-diagonalization-b1.title: B1: A generalized eigenvalue problem
exr-simultaneous-diagonalization-b1.html:
Let A=(1112),B=(2221).

  1. Verify that A≻0 and find the generalized eigenvalues of (A,B).
  2. Find generalized eigenvectors and an invertible S with S⊤AS=I2 and S⊤BS diagonal.

exr-simultaneous-diagonalization-b2.title: B2: Whitening by hand
exr-simultaneous-diagonalization-b2.html: Let A=diag(4,9) and B=(4669). Follow the two steps of the proof of @thm-simultaneous-congruence: compute A−1/2, then C=A−1/2BA−1/2, diagonalize C, and write down S and S⊤BS.

exr-simultaneous-diagonalization-b3.title: B3: A pair that resists
exr-simultaneous-diagonalization-b3.html: Let A=(0110) and B=(1000). Determine whether there is an invertible real S making S⊤AS and S⊤BS both diagonal. Justify your answer.

exr-simultaneous-diagonalization-c1.title: C1: The \A-inner product
exr-simultaneous-diagonalization-c1.title_html: C1: The A-inner product
exr-simultaneous-diagonalization-c1.html:
Let A≻0 and B be self-adjoint in Mn(F), and write ⟨x,y⟩A=y∗Ax.

  1. Prove that ⟨⋅,⋅⟩A is an inner product on Fn.
  2. Prove that T=TA−1B is self-adjoint on (Fn,⟨⋅,⋅⟩A).
  3. Deduce @thm-generalized-eigenvalues-real (a) and (b) from the spectral theorem applied to T, without using @thm-simultaneous-congruence.

exr-simultaneous-diagonalization-c2.title: C2: Signs of the generalized eigenvalues
exr-simultaneous-diagonalization-c2.title_html: C2: Signs of the generalized eigenvalues
exr-simultaneous-diagonalization-c2.html:
Let A≻0 and B be self-adjoint in Mn(F), with generalized eigenvalues d1,…,dn.

  1. Prove that B⪰0 if and only if every di≥0, and B≻0 if and only if every di>0.
  2. Deduce that if A≻0 and B≻0, then detB/detA=∏idi>0.

exr-simultaneous-diagonalization-c3.title: C3: Dropping definiteness of \A
exr-simultaneous-diagonalization-c3.title_html: C3: Dropping definiteness of A
exr-simultaneous-diagonalization-c3.html:
Let A=(1000) and B=(0110), so that A⪰0 but A⊁0.

  1. Compute det(B−λA) and deduce that the pair has no generalized eigenvalues at all.
  2. Prove that no invertible S∈M2(R) makes S⊤AS and S⊤BS both diagonal.

Hint for (b): compare the degree in λ of det(B−λA) on both sides.

exr-singular-value-decomposition-a1.title: A1
exr-singular-value-decomposition-a1.html:
1. Define the singular values of a matrix A∈Mm×n(F). How many are there?
  2. State the singular value decomposition, with the size and the defining property of each factor.
  3. True or false: the singular values of A are the absolute values of its eigenvalues. Justify your answer.
  4. How many non-zero singular values does A have, and why?
  5. Given a compact singular value decomposition A=∑i≤rσiuivi∗, write down orthonormal bases of all four fundamental subspaces of A.
  6. True or false: in A=UΣV∗ the three factors are determined by A. Justify your answer.

exr-singular-value-decomposition-b1.title: B1: A 2 by 2 decomposition
exr-singular-value-decomposition-b1.html: Find a singular value decomposition A=UΣV⊤ of A=(3045)∈M2(R), and compare the singular values with the eigenvalues of A.

exr-singular-value-decomposition-b2.title: B2: When the left singular vectors must be padded
exr-singular-value-decomposition-b2.title_html: B2: When the left singular vectors must be padded
exr-singular-value-decomposition-b2.html: Find a singular value decomposition of A=(100110)∈M3×2(R), saying explicitly where the padding step of @thm-svd is used.

exr-singular-value-decomposition-b3.title: B3: Compact form and the four subspaces
exr-singular-value-decomposition-b3.title_html: B3: Compact form and the four subspaces
exr-singular-value-decomposition-b3.html: For A=(221122)∈M3×2(R), find the compact singular value decomposition A=∑i≤rσiuivi⊤, and hence orthonormal bases of all four fundamental subspaces.

exr-singular-value-decomposition-b4.title: B4: Determine whether
exr-singular-value-decomposition-b4.html:
Determine which of the following statements are correct. For those that are correct, prove them; for those that are not, give a counterexample.

  1. If every eigenvalue of A∈Mn(C) is 0, then every singular value of A is 0.
  2. σi(cA)=|c|σi(A) for every scalar c.
  3. σi(A2)=σi(A)2 for every square A.
  4. A is invertible if and only if n=m and every singular value of A is non-zero.

exr-singular-value-decomposition-c1.title: C1: The Frobenius norm and the largest singular value
exr-singular-value-decomposition-c1.title_html: C1: The Frobenius norm and the largest singular value
exr-singular-value-decomposition-c1.html:
Let A∈Mm×n(F) with singular values σ1≥⋯≥σp.

  1. The text obtained ‖A‖F2=∑i=1pσi2 from unitary invariance. Prove it a second way, directly from ‖A‖F2=tr(A∗A) and the eigenvalues of A∗A, without invoking @lem-frobenius-unitarily-invariant.
  2. Deduce that σ1≤‖A‖F, and determine exactly when equality holds.

exr-singular-value-decomposition-c2.title: C2: The adjoint and the determinant
exr-singular-value-decomposition-c2.title_html: C2: The adjoint and the determinant
exr-singular-value-decomposition-c2.html:
Let A∈Mm×n(F).

  1. Prove that A and A∗ have the same non-zero singular values, with the same multiplicities.
  2. Suppose m=n. Prove that |detA|=σ1σ2⋯σn.
  3. Hence give a formula for |detA| in terms of A∗A only, and check it on A=(3045).

exr-singular-value-decomposition-c3.title: C3: Singular values equal to eigenvalue moduli
exr-singular-value-decomposition-c3.title_html: C3: Singular values equal to eigenvalue moduli
exr-singular-value-decomposition-c3.html:
Let A∈Mn(C) have eigenvalues λ1,…,λn listed with algebraic multiplicity and ordered so that |λ1|≥⋯≥|λn|.

  1. Prove that if A is normal, then σi(A)=|λi| for every i.
  2. Prove the converse: if σi(A)=|λi| for every i, then A is normal.

Hint for (b): compare two expressions for ‖A‖F2.

exr-square-roots-and-cholesky-a1.title: A1
exr-square-roots-and-cholesky-a1.html:
1. State what A1/2 is, including the two conditions that pin it down.
  2. Define |A| for A∈Mm×n(F) and say what size it is.
  3. State the Cholesky factorization theorem.
  4. True or false: every Hermitian matrix has exactly one Hermitian square root. Justify your answer.
  5. Explain in one sentence why the Cholesky algorithm is a test for positive definiteness.

exr-square-roots-and-cholesky-b1.title: B1: Square roots
exr-square-roots-and-cholesky-b1.html:
Compute A1/2 for each of the following, and in each case give a polynomial p with p(A)=A1/2.

  1. A=(5445).
  2. A=(10−6−610).

exr-square-roots-and-cholesky-b2.title: B2: Cholesky, and a planted failure
exr-square-roots-and-cholesky-b2.title_html: B2: Cholesky, and a planted failure
exr-square-roots-and-cholesky-b2.html:
1. Find the Cholesky factor of A=(12−1251−1114), and hence write down detA.
  2. Run the same algorithm on A′=(12−1251−119) and say what the outcome proves.

exr-square-roots-and-cholesky-b3.title: B3: An absolute value
exr-square-roots-and-cholesky-b3.html: Let A=(1111)∈M2(R). Compute |A|, verify ‖|A|x‖=‖Ax‖ directly, and determine whether |A|=A.

exr-square-roots-and-cholesky-c1.title: C1: The trace of a product of positive matrices
exr-square-roots-and-cholesky-c1.title_html: C1: The trace of a product of positive matrices
exr-square-roots-and-cholesky-c1.html:
Let A,B∈Mn(F) with A⪰0 and B⪰0.

  1. Prove that tr(AB)=tr(A1/2BA1/2), and deduce that tr(AB)≥0.
  2. Prove that tr(AB)=0 if and only if AB=0.

Hint for (b): a positive semidefinite matrix of trace 0 is 0.

exr-square-roots-and-cholesky-c2.title: C2: Commuting positive matrices
exr-square-roots-and-cholesky-c2.html:
Let A∈Mn(F) with A⪰0.

  1. Prove without using @thm-psd-square-root (a) that if BA=AB, then BA1/2=A1/2B. Hint: show that B maps each eigenspace of A into itself.
  2. Let B⪰0 with AB=BA. Prove that AB⪰0 and that (AB)1/2=A1/2B1/2.

exr-square-roots-and-cholesky-c3.title: C3: Why definiteness is needed
exr-square-roots-and-cholesky-c3.html:
1. Give a positive semidefinite A∈M2(R), not positive definite, together with two different lower triangular L satisfying A=LL⊤. Which hypothesis of @thm-cholesky fails?
  2. Prove that if A⪰0 then A+tI≻0 for every real t>0, and hence that every positive semidefinite matrix is a limit of positive definite ones in the entrywise sense.

exr-the-loewner-order-a1.title: A1
exr-the-loewner-order-a1.html:
1. Define A⪰B, and say on which set of matrices the relation is defined.
  2. Determine whether the following statement is correct, and justify your answer: for Hermitian A,B, either A⪰B or B⪰A.
  3. Determine whether the following statement is correct, and justify your answer: A⪰B implies aij≥bij for all i,j.
  4. State what fails when both sides of A⪰B⪰0 are squared, and what happens instead when both sides have their square roots taken.
  5. Which clause of @thm-loewner-basic reverses an inequality, and what is the analogous fact about real numbers?

exr-the-loewner-order-b1.title: B1: Decide the relation
exr-the-loewner-order-b1.html:
For each pair of real symmetric matrices, determine whether A⪰B, whether B⪰A, or neither. Justify your answer.

  1. A=(3113), B=I2.
  2. A=(2001), B=(1111).
  3. A=(1003), B=(2001).

exr-the-loewner-order-b2.title: B2: The order reverses
exr-the-loewner-order-b2.html: Let A=(3113) and B=(2112). Verify that A⪰B≻0, compute A−1 and B−1, and check @thm-loewner-basic (d) directly. Check the determinant clause as well.

exr-the-loewner-order-b3.title: B3: Another failure of squaring
exr-the-loewner-order-b3.html: Let A=(3111) and B=(1111). Verify that A⪰B⪰0, and exhibit a vector x with x⊤(A2−B2)x<0.

exr-the-loewner-order-c1.title: C1: When squaring does work
exr-the-loewner-order-c1.html:
Let A,B∈Mn(F) with A⪰B⪰0 and AB=BA.

  1. Prove that if P,Q⪰0 and PQ=QP, then PQ⪰0.
  2. Deduce that A2⪰B2.
  3. Deduce that Ak⪰Bk for every integer k≥1.

Hint for (a): P1/2 is a polynomial in P.

exr-the-loewner-order-c2.title: C2: Kernels and ranks
exr-the-loewner-order-c2.html:
Let A,B∈Mn(F) with A⪰B⪰0.

  1. Prove that nul(A)⊆nul(B).
  2. Deduce that rankA≥rankB.
  3. Give an example with A⪰B⪰0 and rankA=rankB but A≠B.

Hint for (a): pair Ax=0 with x, then use B1/2.

exr-the-loewner-order-c3.title: C3: Largest eigenvalue of a sum
exr-the-loewner-order-c3.title_html: C3: Largest eigenvalue of a sum
exr-the-loewner-order-c3.html:
Let A,B∈Mn(F) be Hermitian.

  1. Prove that λ1(A)I⪰A, and deduce λ1(A+B)≤λ1(A)+λ1(B).
  2. Deduce that if A⪰B, then 0≤λ1(A)−λ1(B)≤λ1(A−B).

lem-det-psd-increment.title: Adding a positive matrix does not decrease the determinant
lem-det-psd-increment.title_html: Adding a positive matrix does not decrease the determinant
lem-det-psd-increment.html:
Let P,Q∈Mn(F) with P≻0 and Q⪰0. Then

det(P+Q)≥detP>0,

with equality if and only if Q=0.

lem-det-shift-principal-minors.title: Shifting by t\I, minor by minor
lem-det-shift-principal-minors.title_html: Shifting by tI, minor by minor
lem-det-shift-principal-minors.html: Let A∈Mn(F) and t∈F. Then det(A+tIn)=∑k=0nEk(A)tn−k, where E0(A)=1 and, for 1≤k≤n, Ek(A)=∑|I|=kdetAI,I is the sum of all k×k principal minors of A.

lem-extreme-eigenvalues-quadratic-form.title: The extreme eigenvalues as extreme values
lem-extreme-eigenvalues-quadratic-form.title_html: The extreme eigenvalues as extreme values
lem-extreme-eigenvalues-quadratic-form.html: Let A∈Mn(F) be Hermitian. Then for every x∈Fn with ‖x‖=1, λn(A) ≤ ⟨Ax,x⟩ ≤ λ1(A), and both bounds are attained, at unit eigenvectors for λn(A) and λ1(A) respectively.

lem-frobenius-sum-of-squares.title: The Frobenius norm counts singular values
lem-frobenius-sum-of-squares.title_html: The Frobenius norm counts singular values
lem-frobenius-sum-of-squares.html: Let A∈Mm×n(F) have singular values σ1≥⋯≥σp. Then (the first identity is the one Section 8 already obtained, recorded here with a label because the proof of the main theorem uses it repeatedly) ‖A‖F2=∑i=1pσi2,‖A−Ak‖F2=∑i>kσi2 for every 0≤k≤p.

lem-gram-bordered.title: Bordering a Gram matrix
lem-gram-bordered.html: Let (v1,…,vk) be a list in an inner product space V, let U=span(v1,…,vk), and let w∈V. Then detG(v1,…,vk,w)=detG(v1,…,vk)⋅d(w,U)2.

lem-hadamard-rank-one.title: Entrywise product of two rank-one positive matrices
lem-hadamard-rank-one.title_html: Entrywise product of two rank-one positive matrices
lem-hadamard-rank-one.html:
Let u,w∈Fn. Then

(uu∗)∘(ww∗)=(u∘w)(u∘w)∗.

lem-orthonormal-capture-bound.title: An orthonormal list captures at most the leading singular values
lem-orthonormal-capture-bound.title_html: An orthonormal list captures at most the leading singular values
lem-orthonormal-capture-bound.html: Let A∈Mm×n(F) with singular values σ1≥⋯≥σp, extended by σi=0 for p<i≤m. Let q1,…,qs be an orthonormal list in Fm, so that s≤m. Then ∑j=1s‖A∗qj‖2 ≤ ∑i=1sσi2.

prp-absolute-value-properties.title: What the absolute value preserves
prp-absolute-value-properties.html: Let A∈Mm×n(F). Then for every x∈Fn, ‖|A|x‖=‖Ax‖. Consequently nul|A|=nulA and rank|A|=rankA.

prp-block-psd-general.title: The Semidefinite Block Criterion
prp-block-psd-general.html: Let A∈Mk(F) and C∈Ml(F) be self-adjoint and put M=(ABB∗C)∈Mk+l(F). Then M⪰0 if and only if A⪰0, every column of B lies in col(A), and C−B∗A+B⪰0.

prp-complex-positivity-forces-hermitian.title: Over \nC, positivity implies Hermitian
prp-complex-positivity-forces-hermitian.title_html: Over C, positivity implies Hermitian
prp-complex-positivity-forces-hermitian.html: Let A∈Mn(C) satisfy ⟨Ax,x⟩∈R for every x∈Cn — in particular, let ⟨Ax,x⟩≥0 for every x. Then A∗=A.

prp-congruence-positivity.title: Congruence preserves positivity
prp-congruence-positivity.html:
Let A∈Mn(F) be Hermitian and S∈Mn×m(F). Then S∗AS∈Mm(F) is Hermitian, and:

  1. if A⪰0, then S∗AS⪰0;
  2. if A≻0 and nul(S)={0}, then S∗AS≻0. In particular, for m=n and S invertible, A≻0 if and only if S∗AS≻0.

prp-loewner-partial-order.title: The Loewner order is a partial order
prp-loewner-partial-order.title_html: The Loewner order is a partial order
prp-loewner-partial-order.html: On the set of Hermitian matrices in Mn(F), the relation ⪰ is reflexive, transitive and antisymmetric: A⪰A; if A⪰B and B⪰C then A⪰C; and if A⪰B and B⪰A then A=B.

prp-pseudoinverse-well-defined.title: The pseudoinverse does not depend on the decomposition
prp-pseudoinverse-well-defined.title_html: The pseudoinverse does not depend on the decomposition
prp-pseudoinverse-well-defined.html:
Let A∈Mm×n(F) and let A=UΣV∗ be any singular value decomposition (@thm-svd). Then X=VΣ+U∗ is the unique matrix in Mn×m(F) such that

  1. for every y∈col(A), Xy is the unique vector of col(A∗) that A sends to y;
  2. Xy=0 for every y∈col(A)⊥.

In particular A+ depends on A alone.

prp-square-root-monotone.title: The square root is order preserving
prp-square-root-monotone.title_html: The square root is order preserving
prp-square-root-monotone.html: Let A,B∈Mn(F) with A⪰B⪰0. Then A1/2⪰B1/2.

thm-block-psd-schur.title: Positive Definiteness Block by Block
thm-block-psd-schur.html:
Let k,l≥1 and let

M=(ABB∗C)∈Mk+l(F)

be Hermitian, with A∈Mk(F), B∈Mk×l(F) and C∈Ml(F).

  1. If M⪰0, then A⪰0 and C⪰0. If M≻0, then A≻0 and C≻0.
  2. Suppose A≻0. Then A is invertible, the Schur complement M/A=C−B∗A−1B∈Ml(F) is Hermitian, and M≻0⟺M/A≻0,M⪰0⟺M/A⪰0.

thm-cholesky.title: Cholesky Factorization
thm-cholesky.html: Let A∈Mn(F) be Hermitian. Then A≻0 if and only if A=LL∗ for some lower triangular L∈Mn(F) whose diagonal entries are real and strictly positive. In that case L is unique.

thm-compact-svd.title: Compact Singular Value Decomposition
thm-compact-svd.html: Let A∈Mm×n(F) have rank r and let A=UΣV∗ be as in @thm-svd, with columns u1,…,um and v1,…,vn. Then A=∑i=1rσiuivi∗, a sum of r matrices of rank 1. Equivalently A=UrΣrVr∗, where Ur∈Mm×r(F) and Vr∈Mn×r(F) hold the first r columns of U and V, and Σr=diag(σ1,…,σr) is square and invertible.

thm-eckart-young.title: Eckart–Young Theorem, Frobenius case
thm-eckart-young.html: Let A∈Mm×n(F) with singular values σ1≥⋯≥σp, and let 0≤k≤p. Then for every B∈Mm×n(F) with rankB≤k, ‖A−B‖F ≥ (∑i>kσi2)1/2, and equality holds for B=Ak. In words: the truncation Ak minimizes ‖A−B‖F over all matrices of rank at most k, and the minimum value is (∑i>kσi2)1/2.

thm-generalized-eigenvalues-real.title: The Definite Generalized Eigenvalue Problem
thm-generalized-eigenvalues-real.html:
Let A,B∈Mn(F) be self-adjoint with A≻0, and let S and D=diag(d1,…,dn) be as in @thm-simultaneous-congruence, with columns s1,…,sn of S. Then:

  1. Bsi=diAsi for every i, and si∗Asj=δij: the columns of S are a basis of Fn of generalized eigenvectors, orthonormal for the inner product ⟨x,y⟩A=y∗Ax;
  2. the generalized eigenvalues of (A,B) are exactly d1,…,dn, all real, and det(B−λA)=1|detS|2∏i=1n(di−λ);
  3. A−1B=SDS−1; in particular A−1B is diagonalizable with real eigenvalues d1,…,dn, although it need not be self-adjoint.

thm-gram-determinant-volume.title: The Gram Determinant Is the Squared Volume
thm-gram-determinant-volume.title_html: The Gram Determinant Is the Squared Volume
thm-gram-determinant-volume.html: Let (v1,…,vk) be a list in an inner product space over F. Then detG(v1,…,vk)=vol(v1,…,vk)2. In particular, if A∈Mm×k(F) has columns v1,…,vk∈Fm, then vol(v1,…,vk)=det(A∗A).

thm-gram-distance-formula.title: Distance by Gram Determinants
thm-gram-distance-formula.html: Let U be a finite-dimensional subspace of an inner product space V, let (v1,…,vk) be a basis of U, and let w∈V. Then d(w,U)2=detG(v1,…,vk,w)detG(v1,…,vk).

thm-gram-iff-psd.title: Gram Matrices Are Exactly the Positive Semidefinite Matrices
thm-gram-iff-psd.title_html: Gram Matrices Are Exactly the Positive Semidefinite Matrices
thm-gram-iff-psd.html:
Let G∈Mk(F). The following are equivalent.

  1. G is the Gram matrix of some list of k vectors in some inner product space over F;
  2. G is the Gram matrix of some list of k vectors in Fr with the standard inner product, where r=rankG;
  3. G⪰0.

Moreover the list is unique up to an isometry: if (v1,…,vk) in V and (w1,…,wk) in W have the same Gram matrix, then there is an isometry from span(v1,…,vk) onto span(w1,…,wk) carrying vj to wj for every j.

thm-hadamard-inequality.title: Hadamard’s Inequality
thm-hadamard-inequality.html:
1. Let A∈Mn(F) with A⪰0. Then detA≤a11a22⋯ann, with equality if and only if A is diagonal or some aii=0.
  2. Let B∈Mn(F) have columns b1,…,bn. Then |detB|≤‖b1‖‖b2‖⋯‖bn‖, with equality if and only if the columns are pairwise orthogonal or some column is 0.

thm-idempotent-canonical-form.title: Canonical Form of an Idempotent in an Orthonormal Basis
thm-idempotent-canonical-form.title_html: Canonical Form of an Idempotent in an Orthonormal Basis
thm-idempotent-canonical-form.html: Let V be an n-dimensional inner product space over F and let P∈L(V) be a projection of rank r. Let (f1,…,fr) be any orthonormal basis of imP and (fr+1,…,fn) any orthonormal basis of (imP)⊥. Then B=(f1,…,fn) is an orthonormal basis of V, and [P]B=(IrX00) for some X∈Mr×(n−r)(F). Moreover P is an orthogonal projection if and only if X=0.

thm-idempotent-orthogonal-iff-selfadjoin.title: Orthogonal Projections Among the Idempotents
thm-idempotent-orthogonal-iff-selfadjoin.html:
Let V be a finite-dimensional inner product space over F and let P∈L(V) satisfy P2=P. The following are equivalent.

  1. P is the orthogonal projection onto its image: P=PU with U=imP.
  2. kerP=(imP)⊥.
  3. P∗=P.
  4. P is normal.
  5. ‖Pv‖≤‖v‖ for every v∈V.

thm-invertible-tfae-positive.title: Invertible Matrix Theorem, with Positive Definiteness
thm-invertible-tfae-positive.title_html: Invertible Matrix Theorem, with Positive Definiteness
thm-invertible-tfae-positive.html:
Let A∈Mn(F) with F=R or F=C. The following are equivalent, and each is equivalent to each of the conditions of @thm-invertible-tfae, @thm-invertible-tfae-det and @thm-invertible-tfae-eigen.

  1. A is invertible.
  2. A∗A≻0.
  3. AA∗≻0.

For a general A∈Mm×n(F), one always has A∗A⪰0, with A∗A≻0 if and only if the columns of A are linearly independent.

thm-loewner-basic.title: Basic Properties of the Loewner Order
thm-loewner-basic.title_html: Basic Properties of the Loewner Order
thm-loewner-basic.html:
Let A,B∈Mn(F) be Hermitian with A⪰B. Then:

  1. S∗AS⪰S∗BS for every S∈Mn×m(F);
  2. λ1(A)≥λ1(B) and λn(A)≥λn(B);
  3. if moreover B⪰0, then trA≥trB and detA≥detB;
  4. if moreover B≻0, then A≻0 and B−1⪰A−1.

thm-oppenheim.title: Oppenheim’s Inequality
thm-oppenheim.html:
Let A,B∈Mn(F) with A⪰0 and B⪰0. Then

det(A∘B) ≥ detA⋅b11b22⋯bnn.

thm-pd-characterizations.title: Characterizations of Positive Definiteness, with Sylvester’s Criterion
thm-pd-characterizations.title_html: Characterizations of Positive Definiteness, with Sylvester’s Criterion
thm-pd-characterizations.html:
Let A∈Mn(F) be Hermitian, and for 1≤k≤n let Ak be its leading principal submatrix, the top-left k×k corner. The following are equivalent.

  1. A≻0.
  2. Every eigenvalue of A is a positive real number.
  3. A=B∗B for some invertible B∈Mn(F).
  4. (Sylvester’s criterion) detAk>0 for every k=1,…,n.

thm-penrose-conditions.title: The Penrose Conditions
thm-penrose-conditions.html:
Let A∈Mm×n(F). Then X=A+ is the unique matrix in Mn×m(F) satisfying all four of

  1. AXA=A;
  2. XAX=X;
  3. (AX)∗=AX;
  4. (XA)∗=XA.

thm-polar-decomposition.title: Polar Decomposition
thm-polar-decomposition.html: Let A∈Mn(C). Then there is a unitary W∈Mn(C) with A=W|A|. The positive semidefinite factor |A| is determined by A. The unitary factor W is determined by A if and only if A is invertible, and then W=A|A|−1. Moreover the same W satisfies the right-handed identity A=|A∗|W,|A∗|=W|A|W∗.

thm-psd-characterizations.title: Characterizations of Positive Semidefiniteness
thm-psd-characterizations.html:
Let A∈Mn(F) be Hermitian. The following are equivalent.

  1. A⪰0.
  2. Every eigenvalue of A is a non-negative real number.
  3. A=B∗B for some B∈Mn(F).
  4. A=C2 for exactly one C∈Mn(F) with C⪰0.
  5. Every principal minor of A is ≥0.

thm-psd-square-root.title: The Positive Square Root
thm-psd-square-root.html:
Let A∈Mn(F) with A⪰0. Then there is exactly one C∈Mn(F) with C⪰0 and C2=A. We write C=A1/2, also A. Moreover:

  1. A1/2=p(A) for some polynomial p with real coefficients (the nodes λi and the values λi are real, so the interpolation of @thm-lagrange-interpolation may be run over R, and R[x]⊆C[x]);
  2. A1/2B=BA1/2 for every B∈Mn(F) with AB=BA;
  3. nul(A1/2)=nul(A) and rankA1/2=rankA; in particular A1/2 is invertible if and only if A is.

The eigenvalues of A1/2 are the non-negative square roots of those of A, with the same eigenvectors.

thm-pseudoinverse-least-squares.title: The pseudoinverse solves both problems at once
thm-pseudoinverse-least-squares.title_html: The pseudoinverse solves both problems at once
thm-pseudoinverse-least-squares.html:
Let A∈Mm×n(F) and b∈Fm, and put x+=A+b. Then:

  1. x+ is a least-squares solution of Ax=b, that is, ‖Ax+−b‖≤‖Az−b‖ for every z∈Fn;
  2. ‖x+‖<‖x‖ for every other least-squares solution x;
  3. if Ax=b is consistent, x+ is its minimum-norm solution in the sense of @thm-minimum-norm-solution; if A is invertible, x+=A−1b.

thm-pseudoinverse-properties.title: Properties of the pseudoinverse
thm-pseudoinverse-properties.html:
Let A∈Mm×n(F). Then:

  1. AA+=Pcol(A) and A+A=Pcol(A∗), the orthogonal projections onto the column space of A in Fm and onto the column space of A∗ in Fn;
  2. (A+)+=A;
  3. (A+)∗=(A∗)+;
  4. rankA+=rankA;
  5. A+=A−1 if A is invertible; A+=(A∗A)−1A∗ if rankA=n; and A+=A∗(AA∗)−1 if rankA=m.

thm-schur-product.title: Schur Product Theorem
thm-schur-product.html:
Let A,B∈Mn(F).

  1. If A⪰0 and B⪰0, then A∘B⪰0.
  2. If A≻0 and B≻0, then A∘B≻0.

thm-simultaneous-congruence.title: Diagonalizing Two Forms by Congruence
thm-simultaneous-congruence.html: Let A,B∈Mn(F) be self-adjoint with A≻0. Then there is an invertible S∈Mn(F) with S∗AS=InandS∗BS=D for some real diagonal D. Over R, with A,B symmetric, S may be taken real.

thm-singular-values-unique.title: The Singular Values Are Determined
thm-singular-values-unique.html:
Let A∈Mm×n(F) and suppose A=UΣV∗ with U,V unitary and Σ∈Mm×n(R) of the shape in @thm-svd, with diagonal entries s1≥⋯≥sp≥0. Then si=σi(A) for every i. Moreover:

  1. the columns of V are forced to be an orthonormal basis of Fn consisting of eigenvectors of A∗A, with A∗Avi=σi2vi for every i≤n, where σi:=0 for p<i≤n; and any such basis occurs;
  2. once V is chosen, ui=Avi/σi is forced for every i≤r=rankA, while ur+1,…,um may be any orthonormal basis of (imA)⊥.

thm-svd.title: Singular Value Decomposition
thm-svd.html: Let A∈Mm×n(F), let p=min(m,n) and let σ1≥⋯≥σp≥0 be its singular values. Then there are unitary matrices U∈Mm(F) and V∈Mn(F) such that A=UΣV∗, where Σ∈Mm×n(R) has (Σ)ii=σi for i=1,…,p and every other entry 0. Moreover the number of non-zero σi equals rankA.

thm-takagi.title: Takagi’s Factorization
thm-takagi.html: Let A∈Mn(C) be symmetric, A⊤=A, with singular values σ1≥⋯≥σn≥0. Then there is a unitary U∈Mn(C) with A=UΣU⊤,Σ=diag(σ1,…,σn).
